title: How Big a Step: The Error in One Step of Motion, and Two Ways to Take It Down

questions.question: A robot drives a circle using the step of lesson 00-05, which points along the heading at the start of each step. What happens?
options: It runs a little wide at every step, always the same way, so the errors add up
questions.explanation: The radius from the centre was bigger than 1 at every step count.

questions.question: The 00-05 step missed a quarter circle by 111.110 mm in 10 steps. What does it miss by in 20?
options: 55.541 mm: twice the steps, half the error
questions.explanation: It needed 1111 steps to be within a millimetre.

questions.question: Which heading does the midpoint step use to move?
options: The average of the wheel speeds
The one halfway through the step, since the start is too early and the end too late by equal amounts
questions.explanation: Twice the steps then gives a quarter of the error, and 13 steps were enough for a millimetre.

questions.question: With 10 steps the 00-05 step missed by 111.110 mm. How did the midpoint step do?
questions.explanation: The cost is one extra addition per step.

questions.question: Why does the exact arc step have to treat going straight separately?
options: The radius is forward divided by the turn, so a zero turn is a division by zero, and a tiny one is the difference of two nearly equal numbers
questions.explanation: Below a turn of 1e-9 it moves forward along the heading.

questions.question: When is the exact arc not the right choice?
options: When the wheel speeds change during the step, which a real robot's do every control cycle, so the step has to be short anyway
questions.explanation: Then the midpoint step is about as good, and it extends to cases with no circle formula.
